timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hi, this is Omni-Rut Westeism with Cape Town University Medicine. Today talking about basic
suturing techniques and showing you three example sutures often used in suturing skin wounds.
First, let's talk about the equipment that is required. The minimum equipment you will
need to suture a wound is suture material. There are many different kinds of suture material
available on the market and a full discussion of their pros and cons are outside the scope of
this demonstration. Today we will use a nylon monofilament suture. You will also need a needle holder,
a pair of scissors and either tooth or non-toothed foreseps depending on what's available.
You will need local anesthetic to anesthetize the wound, some goes and a cleaning solution.
After explaining the procedure to the patient, don universal precautions and proceed gently cleaning
the external surface of the wound. Once this is been done, inject local anesthetic along the wound
edges, approaching the wound from the wound side itself and not injecting through the skin.
Make sure that the entire wound is anesthetized along both its lengths from edge to edge.
Once the wound has been anesthetized, safely dispose of your shot and allow the local anesthetic
enough time to work. After an appropriate passage of time, taste the wound edge and confirm that
your anesthesia has been successful. It is now appropriate to clean the wound a bit more vigorously,
including the inside of the wound and to rinse or irrigate the antiface any far more material.
This should now cause less discomfort to the patient. Once the skin has been prepared,
proceed to suturing. In this case, we are going to use a nylon monofilament suture.
Open your suture, reveal the needle and grab the needle with your needle holder.
Hold the needle about a third to a quarter from the back of the needle on the flat surface with
a tip of the needle holder. This allows for an easier rotating motion of the wrist
to take the needle through the skin. When suturing a wound, we suggest starting in the middle
and then progressively halving the gaps in between to ensure even distribution of sutures.
